title: News publisher files class action antitrust suit against Google, citing AI’s harms to their bottom line

notes.thought: Helena World Chronicle alleges in a class action filed this week in the U.S. District Court for D.C. that Google and Alphabet engage in anticompetitive conduct violating the Sherman Act and other antitrust laws by siphoning publishers' content, readers and ad revenue.
notes.covers: Opening paragraph: identity of plaintiff, forum, statutes and core allegation.

notes.thought: Helena World Chronicle is an Arkansas-based publisher that owns and publishes two weekly newspapers and is the named plaintiff in the December 2023 class action against Google.
notes.covers: Second paragraph identifying the plaintiff and its business.

notes.thought: The complaint asserts that Google is 'starving the free press' by redistributing publishers' content inside its own products and that the practice costs publishers billions of dollars in lost revenue.
notes.covers: Second paragraph's framing of harm and the 'billions of dollars' characterisation.

notes.thought: Google's Knowledge Graph is a machine-readable fact database launched in May 2012, built by extracting information from publisher websites plus open-source and licensed datasets, and used to populate the Knowledge Panel in search results.
notes.covers: Third and fourth paragraphs describing the Knowledge Graph and its provenance.

notes.thought: When a user searches a topic, Google renders a Knowledge Panel to the right of the organic results and populates it with summaries drawn from the Knowledge Graph, thereby satisfying the query without a visit to the underlying publisher page.
notes.covers: Fourth paragraph quoted from the complaint explaining how the panel is shown and sourced.

notes.thought: By 2020 the Google Knowledge Graph had grown to roughly 500 billion facts describing about 5 billion entities, per figures quoted in the Helena World Chronicle complaint.
notes.covers: Fifth paragraph's scale statistics.

notes.thought: Featured Snippets are Google's algorithmically extracted answer summaries pulled directly from webpages and surfaced above organic results, which the complaint cites as another traffic-diverting mechanism.
notes.covers: Sixth paragraph naming Featured Snippets and their role in the suit.

notes.thought: Search Generative Experience (SGE) is Google's AI-powered conversational search product that answers queries in natural language inside the results page, cited in the suit as aggravating publishers' traffic losses.
notes.covers: First and ninth paragraphs describing SGE.

notes.thought: The complaint contends that SGE is designed to keep users inside Google's 'walled garden' while reusing publishers' content, with the alleged goal of discouraging end-users from visiting the websites of class members in the digital news publishing line of commerce.
notes.covers: Eighth and ninth paragraphs quoting the complaint's SGE characterisation.

notes.thought: Because SGE consumes the same GoogleBot crawler feed as Google's general search, a publisher cannot block SGE without also losing placement in ordinary search results, leaving no clean opt-out option.
notes.covers: Ninth paragraph's point about inability to block SGE and the tenth paragraph's opt-out injunction ask.

notes.thought: The Atlantic modelled a Google search experience integrated with AI and found that in 75% of queries the AI would answer the user without requiring a click-through to The Atlantic's site.
notes.covers: Seventh paragraph's WSJ-reported statistic on The Atlantic's internal modelling.

notes.thought: As reported by The Wall Street Journal using Similarweb data, Google sends roughly 40% of referral traffic to news publishers' websites.
notes.covers: Seventh paragraph's Similarweb figure.

notes.thought: Publishers believe that full rollout of Google's AI search products will cut their website traffic by 20-40%; falsifiable by comparing per-publisher Google referral volume before and after AI-search availability.
notes.covers: Eighth paragraph's WSJ-reported publisher expectation.

notes.thought: The complaint alleges, citing a 2023 News Media Alliance report and a Washington Post article, that Google's Bard chatbot was trained on a dataset that included news, magazine and digital publications.
notes.covers: Eleventh paragraph on Bard's training data.

notes.thought: A Washington Post analysis conducted with the Allen Institute for AI found that News and Media sites form the third-largest category of material used in AI training datasets.
notes.covers: Eleventh paragraph's parenthetical about the Post / Allen Institute research.

notes.thought: The complaint additionally alleges that Google's changes to AdSense rates have harmed publishers economically, positioning the rate changes as one more instance of anticompetitive conduct within the digital news advertising line of commerce.
notes.covers: Twelfth paragraph's mention of AdSense rate changes among the suit's concerns.

notes.thought: The suit alleges Google improperly spoliated evidence by destroying chat messages, an issue previously raised and sustained in Epic Games' app-store antitrust case against Google, which Epic won.
notes.covers: Twelfth paragraph on spoliation and the Epic Games precedent.

notes.thought: In the week of 15 December 2023 German publisher Axel Springer signed a deal with OpenAI to license its news content for use in AI model training, an example of publishers pre-empting the traffic-loss problem.
notes.covers: Eighth paragraph's Axel Springer–OpenAI anecdote.

notes.thought: Under a November 2023 agreement with the Canadian government, Google will pay $73.5 million (C$100 million) each year to Canadian news organisations, distributed according to each outlet's headcount.
notes.covers: Thirteenth paragraph describing the Canadian bargaining-code settlement.

notes.thought: Meta began blocking news content for Canadian users in August 2023 in response to pressure from Canada's new law requiring payment for publisher content, and its own negotiations with Canadian publishers remain unresolved as of December 2023.
notes.covers: Thirteenth paragraph on Meta's parallel Canadian standoff.

notes.thought: Beyond damages, the suit asks the court for injunctions requiring Google to obtain publisher consent before using website data to train general-purpose AI products (Google's own and rivals') and to allow publishers who opt out of SGE to remain visible in ordinary Google search results.
notes.covers: Twelfth paragraph detailing the requested injunctive relief.

notes.thought: Plaintiffs' counsel Hausfeld frames the case as necessary to restore competition in digital news and reference publishing and to set guardrails for the free marketplace of ideas in the AI era, invoking both the Sherman Act and the Clayton Act for class-wide relief.
notes.covers: Penultimate paragraph quoting Hausfeld's website announcement.

notes.thought: A Google spokesperson rejects the Helena World Chronicle suit outright as 'meritless', pushing back against the complaint's central antitrust and AI-training allegations.
notes.covers: Final truncated line containing Google's spokesperson statement.

notes.thought: This note indexes the Google antitrust actions that surrounded the Helena World Chronicle filing in December 2023: the U.S. DOJ digital ad technology monopoly suit, the 2020 DOJ search and search-advertising civil suit, the Epic Games app-store case, and Canada's news-content settlement.
notes.covers: Thirteenth and fourteenth paragraphs on the broader legal and international context.

title: Apple defends Google Search deal in court: ‘There wasn’t a valid alternative’

notes.thought: The Information Services Agreement (ISA) is the contractual arrangement, in place since 2002, that makes Google's search engine the default on Apple's devices in exchange for yearly payments from Google to Apple.
notes.covers: Paragraph 5: definition, vintage and function of the ISA

notes.thought: In the US v. Google context, a default search engine is the engine preselected on a device at setup, which a user must actively change rather than choose, and which Apple fixes to Google through the ISA.
notes.covers: Testimony on iPhone setup and what 'default' means for users

notes.thought: Under the ISA's current form, negotiated by Eddy Cue with Sundar Pichai in 2016, Google pays Apple a percentage of the advertising revenue earned from Apple users it directs to Google Search; Apple pressed for a higher percentage, Google for the status quo, and they settled on an undisclosed figure.
notes.covers: Paragraphs 5-6: parties, consideration and the 2016 renegotiation, with amounts reserved to closed sessions

notes.thought: The Department of Justice's theory of US v. Google holds that Google's cluster of default-engine agreements — with Apple, Samsung, Mozilla and others — produces de facto dominance of search entry points across practically every platform.
notes.covers: Paragraph 8: why default deals are central to the DOJ's case

notes.thought: Cue testified on 2023-09-26 that Apple never seriously considered another provider or building its own search because 'there wasn't a valid alternative to Google at the time' — a claim he said still holds; the warrant is Apple's own product evaluation, and the scope is the 2016 renegotiation period.
notes.covers: Paragraph 7: the no-alternative claim and its stated warrant

notes.thought: Asked by DOJ lawyer Meagan Bellshaw whether Apple would have walked away over the revenue share, Cue testified he never considered that an option, stating it was always in both Google's and Apple's interest to get a deal done.
notes.covers: Paragraph 7: Cue's answer on the walkaway question, open session, 2023-09-26

notes.thought: Cue argued Apple should not present a search-engine chooser during iPhone setup because setup is 'just critical stuff' aimed at getting users running fast, and unfamiliar options would be a poor experience — a claim scoped to first-boot setup, not to settings changes later.
notes.covers: Paragraph 9: 'We try to get people up and running as fast possible' and Cue's inability to name alternatives

notes.thought: Bellshaw's objection to Apple's setup-minimalism defence is that Apple already asks users to decide on font size and appearance, Maps location tracking, and App Tracking Transparency, so search could be one of the choices offered rather than a fixed default.
notes.covers: Paragraph 8: the three setup screenshots and the consistency point Bellshaw drew from them

notes.thought: Against Apple's assertion that users may 'easily' change the default engine, DuckDuckGo's CEO testified in the week before 2023-09-26 that switching away from the default takes too many steps, contesting the friction premise of Apple's defence.
notes.covers: Paragraph 9 parenthetical: the 'easily' dispute and DuckDuckGo CEO testimony

notes.thought: Cue testified on 2023-09-26 that one provision of the ISA required Google to let people search without logging in, and that Apple separately hardened Safari and its platforms against tracking by Google or others.
notes.covers: Paragraph 10: the contractual privacy provision and Safari mitigations

notes.thought: Emails and slides Bellshaw put to Cue on 2023-09-26 show Cue and Apple criticising Google's privacy policies, with Cue agreeing that Apple has 'always thought we had better privacy than Google'.
notes.covers: Paragraph 10: exhibits of Apple's own privacy criticism

notes.thought: The DOJ's unstated but implied claim is that Apple's 'best product' rationale is pretextual: Apple places a company whose privacy practices it publicly disparages at the centre of its platform because the ISA payments are so large, with the warrant drawn from Apple's own exhibits plus its financial filings.
notes.covers: Paragraph 11: the DOJ's implied economics-over-privacy reading of Apple's testimony

notes.thought: Against Bellshaw's point, grounded in Apple's financial filings, that the ISA accounts for a significant portion of Apple's profits, Cue replied that Apple does not look at the money that way because the figure omits the work Apple did to make its platform attractive enough for the deal to perform.
notes.covers: Paragraph 11: the profits question and Cue's reframing

notes.thought: Cue's testimony held two positions simultaneously — that Apple exists to protect user privacy and that Google is the search engine Apple believes in — and the trial treated the compatibility of those two positions as the operative question of 2023-09-26's session.
notes.covers: Paragraph 4: the two messages and the tension between them

notes.thought: Specific ISA revenue-share figures were discussed only in closed court sessions during Apple's 2023-09-26 testimony in US v. Google, leaving the negotiated percentage undisclosed to the public record.
notes.covers: Paragraphs 6 and 12: closed-session handling of the numbers

title: 5 things we learned so far about the Google antitrust case

notes.covers: Description of the history-off option at the centre of the deletion dispute

notes.covers: Second paragraph distinguishing the ad-tech case from the search case

notes.thought: Holding user inertia and lack of switching effort constant, being the preselected search default raises a engine's query volume, while losing default placement reduces it, a relation Google documented internally in 2007.
notes.covers: Causal relation between default/homepage placement and search volume

notes.thought: Under the Google–Apple agreement running since 2003, Google pays Apple for default search placement and in return agrees not to promote Chrome to Safari users, which keeps Apple from switching engines or offering browser choice at setup.
notes.covers: Mutual obligations of the Google–Apple search deal and their effects

notes.thought: Google's executives assert a reinforcing relation in which paying for default placement yields more queries, more query data yields a better engine, and a better engine justifies further default payments; the model is company testimony, not an established fact.
notes.covers: Pichai's justification for default spending via data intake and quality

notes.thought: The Google–Apple default search agreement had been in place since 2003, giving it roughly two decades of duration by the 2023 trial.
notes.covers: Reported start date of the Apple deal

notes.covers: Observed consequences of the Chrome-promotion restriction for Apple users

notes.covers: 2021 chat message in which Pichai requested history-off
